children: Merck

said its experimental eye drug remigromig improved vision in patients with a diabetes-related eye disease, meeting the main goal of a late-stage clinical trial. However, patients receiving the treatment experienced higher rates of a potentially serious eye complication than those taking an established medication.

The results, presented Sunday at the American Academy of Ophthalmology annual meeting in New Orleans, showed that the drug performed comparably to ranibizumab, an existing treatment, in patients with diabetic macular edema. The condition causes swelling in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye, and can lead to vision loss.
The Phase 2b/3 BRUNELLO trial enrolled 984 patients who received one of two doses of Merck's drug or ranibizumab, with injections into the eye every four weeks.

After one year, patients receiving the lower dose of remigromig gained an average of 9.1 letters on a standard eye chart, while those receiving the higher dose gained 8.7 letters. Patients treated with ranibizumab gained 11.8 letters.

Both doses met the trial's primary goal of demonstrating that the experimental treatment was not meaningfully less effective than the established drug. However, neither dose proved superior to ranibizumab on the study's secondary measures.
Safety findings raise questions

Despite the positive results, researchers observed higher rates of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, a serious complication in which abnormal blood vessels grow inside the eye and can cause bleeding or vision loss.
The complication occurred in 6.7% of patients receiving the lower dose and 6.1% of those receiving the higher dose, compared with 0.9% of patients treated with ranibizumab.
Patients receiving Merck's drug were also more likely to stop treatment because of side effects. Discontinuation rates were 4.9% and 4.5% for the two doses, compared with 0.9% for ranibizumab.

Merck said additional analyses are underway to better understand the safety findings. The company suggested that some cases of worsening diabetic eye disease could reflect the natural progression of the condition, although that explanation has not been established.
The company also said the complications were generally manageable with existing treatments.
Different approach to treating vision loss
Remigromig, also known as MK-3000, works differently from widely used eye medications that block a protein called VEGF, which encourages the growth of abnormal blood vessels.
Instead, the experimental treatment activates a biological process known as the Wnt pathway, which helps maintain and repair the protective barrier surrounding blood vessels in the retina.

In diabetic macular edema, damaged blood vessels leak fluid into the central part of the retina, causing swelling that interferes with sharp vision. Merck hopes that strengthening the blood vessels' protective barrier will reduce leakage and help preserve sight.
The approach could offer another option for patients who respond poorly to existing treatments.

"These findings ... support continued evaluation of this novel approach as we look forward to additional Phase 3 results from the BAROLO study," said Dr. Donald D'Amico, chair of ophthalmology at Weill Cornell Medicine and the study's presenting author.
Merck

estimates that nearly 1.6 million Americans have diabetic macular edema. Up to 40% of patients continue to experience disease activity after six months of treatment, highlighting the need for additional therapies.
Merck expands eye disease research
Merck acquired the drug through EyeBio, a biotechnology company that is now a wholly owned subsidiary.
The company plans to discuss the BRUNELLO findings with regulatory authorities while continuing a separate late-stage trial, called BAROLO, involving patients with diabetic macular edema.
Researchers are also evaluating the treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration, another condition that can cause severe vision loss, and swelling associated with blocked retinal veins.
Merck

is developing a second experimental eye drug, MK-8748, that combines two approaches: strengthening blood vessels and blocking VEGF. That treatment is undergoing late-stage testing for diabetic macular edema and wet age-related macular degeneration.

For investors, the BRUNELLO results provide evidence that Merck's approach to treating retinal disease can deliver meaningful improvements in vision. However, the higher rates of serious eye complications could complicate the drug's path toward regulatory approval and commercial adoption.

The upcoming BAROLO results and further safety analyses will help determine whether the treatment can compete with established medications in a market where doctors already have several effective options.
